newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Constantinescu backers scent victory in Romania.
newsitem.headline: Constantinescu backers scent victory in Romania.

text.p: Romanians flocked to vote on Sunday in a close presidential election which could end President Ion Iliescu's seven years in power and symbolically finish the 1989 anti-communist revolt.
Iliescu, a senior official under dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, was locked in a tough fight with Emil Constantinescu, an academic who held no office under communism.

But as voting drew to a close in the country of 23 million, high turnout figures appeared to favour Constantinescu and opposition activists seemed ready to savour a victory that would bring an end to the legacy of communism.

Although no commentator was willing to name a winner after the first round two weeks ago gave the president a slender four-point lead over his challenger, Constantinescu's supporters were quietly confident on Sunday evening.

Officials said turnout by late evening was nearly 72 percent, more than one point higher than in the first round this month. Some polling stations remained open beyond the 9 p.m. (1900 GMT) deadline to take in straggling voters.
Exit polls were to be broadcast after all voting ceased at midnight (2200 GMT).

A particularly high turnout was recorded in ethnic Hungarian areas and big cities, which vote solidly for Constantinescu. Lower turnouts were recorded in rural areas, which traditionally support the president.

Voters signalled they were ready for a change this month by throwing Iliescu's leftist party out of government for the first time since Ceausescu's 1989 overthrow and execution. A new centrist government is to be formed within days.

"If I am elected, I will not only be a new president but a different kind of president," Constantinescu said after being thronged by hundreds of supporters outside a polling station. "A president who will stay in touch with ordinary Romanians."

The opposition says leftists hijacked the 1989 revolution to seize power. They say victory will end Romania's status as the one Eastern European country where anti-communists have not held power and will finally improve the country's image abroad.

"I voted for Emil Constantinescu. I've been waiting for this all my life," Alexandra Negrici, 34, said in Timisoara, the town where the 1989 upheaval started. "If he wins, we will be able to say at last that the revolution has been completed."

City authorities were preparing for the celebrations that would follow Constantinescu's historic triumph with public transport due to run all night in Bucharest to ferry supporters into the city centre.
In the northern town of Baia Mare, hundreds of people gathered in a park, some with small children, to wait for the results, candles lit and portable radios switched on.
Constantinescu, a geology professor, accuses Iliescu of seven years of corrupt mismanagement that has left Romanians in poverty with average monthly salaries of less than $100.

The president vowed during the campaign to shield Romanians against the excesses of market economics and told voters his rival would restore exiled King Michael and pre-war landlords bent on reclaiming their homes and closing factories.
"I believe I can be the best alternative in the present situation. A president needs experience," he said after chatting to voters outside a Bucharest polling station.

If he hangs on for another term, Iliescu will face a hostile cabinet committed to tax cuts and improved benefits combined with financial discipline to bridge the gap in living standards with near neighbours Hungary and Poland.
